utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit. And you may begin, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Witness, can you please tell the Trial Chamber your full name and surname?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: My name is Andelko Dragas.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were born on the 20th of November, 1951?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In the village of Gornji Mrkovici in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You completed your elementary school in Sarajevo. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And the technical high school in Sarajevo too?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You worked for the post and telegraph and telephone company in Sarajevo until 1992?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me show a map right away. This is P194.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the map be enlarged, please, to the east. And if it could be enlarged further still, the eastern side of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you read the place names here?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: Well, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you show us the location of your home in the early days of the conflict and can you tell us since when you had been living there?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: My home was --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please take the pencil?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: Yes, please. Here it is. This larger dot.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you plays the letter K next to it, please.

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know when the conflict broke out in Sarajevo between --

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: The warring parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: On the 4th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Where were you throughout the conflict?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: Throughout the conflict I was a member of the army of the Republika Srpska in the area of responsibility, and if I may be allowed to mark points on the red line.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, please, show us what you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: These two dots stand for the area of responsibility of the unit I belonged to throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And which unit was that, please?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: In the beginning, it was called the 1st Kosevo Brigade. Later on a battalion was formed, which was part of the 3rd Sarajevo Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Where was your position precisely?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: My positions were here I drew a dot which is supposed to be on the red line.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to know where you positions were in relation to a house?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: As you are able to see my house was located from hundred metres behind my positions. This is where my house was and this is where my positions were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please mark that with the letter P?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what this red line represents?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: I presume this to be the line along which the units of the army of Republika Srpska were deployed whereas the blue line stands roughly for the units of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you draw this dot accurately? I think it is drawn on the confrontation line?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: I suppose I did. The map should be zoomed in further my eyesight is not that sharp, but I suppose I roughly marked the confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what was there precisely where this dot is.

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: My trench was there, the trench to which I regularly was deployed. When my unit needed that, I would go all the way to this other red dot here. It depended on the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain for the Bench what the name of this geographical feature is?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: This geographical feature is called Jagomir or the area in general is called Pionirska Dolina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This geographical feature is part of which hill?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: This stands at the foot of the Grdonj hill. It stretches over an a gentle slope in the direction of Hum. I don't think there are other hills in the general area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Which elevation point overlooks the area? And I mean the area where your positions were.

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: Grdonj and Hum hills. These are the highest grounds overlooking that spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At the time of the start of the conflict, did Spicasta Stijena, a geographical feature, mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: I heard of Spicasta Stijena during the war and after the war. I'm very familiar with the area, as I would cross that particular stretch on my way to Gornji Mrkovici -- on my way to Gornji Mrkovici to my school in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you draw us the line which in peacetime -- can you draw a line standing for the route which you took on your way to school in peacetime?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Does this mean that at the time you attended elementary school you did not reside in the house where you resided at the start of the war?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: No. I was born in Gornji Mrkovici and that is where I lived until 1967 when my parents moved to the location I marked earlier on. I completed my primary education and the first year of my high school before we moved to that location in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You spent the entire war in the trenches there in the vicinity of your home?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, until the Dayton Accords were signed and-- actually, sometime after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now that you mention it, what happened after the Dayton Accords were signed?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: When the Dayton Accords were signed, we moved to Rudo municipality. We only took a couple of our belongings, the essential ones that could fit in a truck. We spent five years there before we returned to the location called Hres.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But you never went back to your house again?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: No, never again. Let me tell you that went to see my house on several occasions and tried to repair it, to repair the damage that was inflicted on my house, but every time I went back to it, I found new, fresh damage there, and eventually I thought it was pointless.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell the Judges what events unfolded in this particular area during the war?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: Sarajevo was surrounded by predominantly Serb villages toward the east and west. What we were doing, most of the time, was protecting our own properties and families. A better part of our properties had been abandoned for the sake of creating strong positions, defence positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Behind the trenches where you were, was there anything?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: There was a road in the direction of the east, in the direction of Pale. The army of the Federation had been trying to cut off this particular road because this constituted the only link with the municipalities of Hadzici, Vogosca and Ilidza. For this reason we were intent on defending this particular road with all our might. It had been targeted by all manner of weapons during the war. At one section of this road we placed a cover made of planks and in other places it was only shielded off by a curtain of sorts, merely to shield people from the line of sight of the enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber how often the warring parties clashed around this particular road?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: The attacks were very, very frequent and they intensified as the war continued. I'm thinking from the start, you could say towards the end of it. I cannot really tell you now the number of the attacks. The truces didn't really mean that much. It didn't mean that it would be quiet. There were very few times when it was actually a truce. So the attacks on the lines there were very intense throughout. I can tell you that visits from relatives continued, and then when they saw how close the lines of separation were and when they saw the constant shooting, they were surprised. They said in our area, the lines are about 5 kilometres apart, so it's much more quiet in our area than it is here in yours. That's what they used to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to show you a photograph later, actually a document from the Prosecution, P361, but as long as we have the map in front of us, you -- you said that as the war was drawing to an end, the fighting became more and more intense?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So can we now focus on 1994. Can you please tell us what the situation was in 1994, in the second half of 1994?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: As I said, the fighting intensified. Sometimes we had to leave some positions because we couldn't defend them, and then later, with the help of units from the left and the right, we would retake them and go back to positions that we previously held. At one point, I recall when I was engaged --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Just one moment. Thank you. Can you please tell the Judges where the clashes occurred most frequently, at which positions?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: The road that is closest to the separation line was at Barice. That would be here. Should I put a dot there or something?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: A circle, small circle.

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You can mark that with a letter B, please.

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And can you please tell us if there was some kind of building there next to the ground?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: There was a fort there. It was called Mala Tvrdjava, the small fort. It was built in the Austro-Hungarian period. And it was a facility built of stone, very strong. And it was conceived to be as a surveillance facility to be used in the defence of the town, according to the strategy of the Austro-Hungarians. At the time we held that facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. None of this is in the transcript. I interrupted him. Nothing of this that he said is in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In that case, Witness, would you repeat what you just said?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What you said about the fort, the tower.

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: It was a fort or a tower called Mala Kula, Mala Tvrdjava. It was built of strong stone. It wasn't very large and the tower was in our hands at the time it was built during the Austro-Hungarian times as an observation point to be used in the defence of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did it ever go to the hands of the enemy?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: Yes, I think it passed into the hands of the enemy in 1994 during intense fighting. It could not be defended so it was abandoned.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell me if you know when General Dragomir Milosevic became the commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact date, but I remember that he did come and that he was the commander of the SRK. And I saw him twice from very close-up.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You just mentioned that -- I'm going to have to pay attention. You are quite good and you're speaking thoroughly and slowly, but I'm not functioning today, it seems. So please tell me, at one point you said that this tower in the second half of that year passed into the hands of --

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: The army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Now I would like the Judges to help me to save the map in this form, like this as an exhibit, because I will later have to go back to the same map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D255, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness now be shown document D156. This last part of the document in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First, Witness, can you look at the heading of the document and the date, please. And can you please read who the heading of the document refers to? Could you please read the heading of the document?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: Are you talking to me?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, command of the 1st Corps and then there is the number 05/4-266.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, so far you were speaking slowly and now you need to continue to speak slowly when you're reading this document.

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: I can repeat. Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina command of the 1st Corps. OP.Number: 05/4-266, date 19th of September, 1994. Daily combat report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now look at the next page to see who signed this document. Can you look at the end of the document?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that. The stamp states 1st Corps and then commander Brigadier-General Vahid Karavelic and there is a signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now go back to the first page and I would like you to look at the paragraph beginning with: "Our forces."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please zoom in on this part in B/C/S, which is under paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And can you please read the beginning?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: The paragraph under number 2?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: "Our forces. 2.1, at the Sarajevo front our forces on the 18th of September, 1994, have been executing combat actions in order to occupy Spicasta Stijena and Mala Kula. For this task, the following forces have been engaged. The strength of one platoon from the 120th Mountain Brigade, Crni Labudovi, the blacks swans, the PTOD platoon of the MUP, in quotes, Bosna, the reconnaissance and sabotage platoon of the 105th Mountain Brigade, the 2nd platoon for intervention of the 105th Mountain Brigade, the pioneer platoon, the engineers platoon of the 2nd Company Reserve, also from the 105th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. There's no need to read everything but perhaps you can look at the last paragraph and tell us what it states there.

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: Yes. "To capture part of the Spicasta Stijena," and that was held until the morning hours. Actually, I apologise. The captured part of Spicasta Stijena has held on up to the evening hours. And then probably the captured part of the fort of Spicasta Stijena held on until the morning hours, probably until 7.00 a.m. And then I can't see what it states here. The second word is: Fierce shelling, a part of Spicasta Stijena was taken with mortar of 82 millimetre, recoilless guns and a PAM.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What I would like to ask you is the following: You already spoke about the fighting in that area on that day and over the two days in question. Did you take part in this fighting, first of all?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. In the re-taking of the fort.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And how did that conflict proceed and how did it end?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: We started firing from the broader area of the fort. The commander Milosevic was there; he was the corps commander. We set off with a large force. There were dead on both sides. In any case, we re-took the fort. One interesting thing happened. The soldiers of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina were afraid for some reason. They were abandoning their weapons and began to run away. Our units wanted us to move the line downwards, because we were frequently under threat, and then we also had some sort of right to that area, because our houses were down below, the property of my countrymen, so we wanted to move the line down towards the town. But to our disappointment, the corps commander at the time said there is no question of that, only go to the original positions, entrench yourself well and do not let them move you anymore. As for further advances, that was out of the question, because the lines of separation had been written down, and they are under the control of international forces, and if we were to do something like that, we would be creating trouble for ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: Well, this statement was not gladly received by the regular soldiers, however, but that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And can you please tell me, if you know, how it came about that the General was there at that location that day?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: Well, I cannot really say, but I know, in general, that there was a sort of title among us soldiers, meaning a drawing room general, meaning a person who would be sitting around drinking coffee and looking at the maps. However, compared to others, this commander was an operational one. He would be touring units to create discipline among the units to prevent anarchy. He would always ask if something was missing, if there was shortages of food, medicine, what the problems of the soldiers were, what could be resolved what could not be resolved. This front was quite a long one so that he would come quite frequently and I remember one occasion, my wife worked as a director of the health centre that belonged to our unit, and the general was touring and he came, and since I came to pick up my wife, I could hear directly. He asked if you had problems in food or medicine, how are you coping, and so on and so forth, and then someone said sejfo, and the general said, Do you have other patients here, non-Serb patients? And there happened to be two Muslims there at the time and one Croat, and he said, And what is -- how are these patients treated, and they said, In the same way, just like everyone else. And he said, Yes, and that's how it should be. There is no need for anybody who had the misfortune to end up here to feel as a second-class citizen. And I have to tell you sincerely that this is something that I was glad to hear. I think that he just spoke out what was my opinion as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I think the narrative has gone on long enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I will note and will object that all of this lengthy testimony that has been given concerning statements and acts by the accused is not on the 65 ter summary of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Carry on, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The summary does indicate that the witness should speak of the events transpiring at this very location. And the witness has just confirmed that the accused in this case was also at his positions and it has to do with the very same fighting that we indicated in the summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could not have known myself whether the general was precisely at that location on that very day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You don't have to deal with it. A summary is what it is says. It is a summary. It doesn't have to be comprehensive. The fact that something is not in the summary doesn't mean that it can't be led in court. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You said that this particular road was very important and that there were constant attempts at cutting off that particular thoroughfare. Did General Dragomir Milosevic pass along that particular road and how often?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: This was the Hadzici-Ilidza-Ilijas-Vogosca road, leading to the headquarters of the corps and it was the only road linking it with this particular location, otherwise the area was a mountainous one, hilly one and not easily traffickable. The road was a necessary evil, to put it that way, since there was no other. How should I put it now properly in military terms. Someone holding a senior officer's rank could perhaps tell you how often they had to travel the road. I suppose in wartime one has to travel -- one had to travel that particular road quite often. If not every day, then every second or third day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You described this particular event here which lasted for one day and through the night into the next morning, as it is indicated here. Were there any such similar events in the area toward the end of 1994?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: Yes, there were. My unit assisted the units holding the Nisici plateau. I was assigned to help them out along the section of the road at Jasan. It was sometime in mid-July, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My question had to do with that very same location where this event took place on the 19th of September.

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: There were similar clashes taking place before that date and after that date. Now, since the entire area ended up in the hands of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina the authorities there in cooperation with their military senior officers, placed various landmarks where they deemed them necessary and even today you can see their special memorial sites.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness please repeat the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, will you please repeat the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The territory where my unit was positioned ended up in the hand of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, according to the Dayton Accords. The current authorities there, in cooperation with the military structures, have been putting up memorial sites in memory of their own fighters. You can see these same memorial sites being placed in the vicinity of Serb homes. I can't recall all these titles used there, but I do recall this one, Amidza.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't believe this to be very important, but the witness said that these memorial sites were placed on Serb properties, but this was entered in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object on the grounds of relevance to the witness's evidence being lead to events that took place after the end of the war, after the Dayton Accords.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that by itself, of course, doesn't make it irrelevant. There may be a connecting factor and I wait now to hear from Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I thought that this would be -- that I would denied the right to lead this evidence, but I believe the witness is saying that Serb soldiers were getting killed in the very spot where today memorial sites stand in the memory of -- of the fighters of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll hear nothing more on this point. Please move on to another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is precisely why I did not wish to put any questions in that direction. Although I do believe it personally significant.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what sort of weapons you had over there, in view of the lie of the terrain?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: We mostly had light infantry weapons. This was purely for practical reasons. Had we had heavy artillery pieces, ones which require vehicles to tow them. The general terrain was quite unfavourable for that. In the event the road were to be cut off, we would not be able to pull the military hardware out. I suppose that this was the reason why the superior military structures decided that we should not have any. We had semi-automatic rifles, automatic rifles, infantry weapons, in short.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any sort of support from weapons that you yourselves did not have?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: Well, probably this went both ways. I suppose that both on our side people were getting killed, as were people getting killed on the other side from shells and fire weapons. I know that in 1994 Djordje Jesic, Safka Radzenovic, Nedjo Grujic, all of them were killed from shells. And I believe that they were more than five kilometres away from the line of separation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Which infantry weapons did you have in the trenches?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: We had rifles, we had light machine-guns, we had M48 rifles, we had M74 automatic rifles, semi-automatic rifles, M73 light machine-guns. The sort of weapons any unit engaged in active combat would have. We had hand-grenades, rifle-launched grenades.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, did you have snipers in your unit and did you need them at that very location?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: The lines of separation were such in our general area that the two armies were opposite each other. To my mind, a sniper would make no difference, because no infantry weapons were able to hit their target, in fact. If you look at the map of Poljine where the Kosevo Brigade was deployed all the way through to the junction at Smreka. Every neighbourhood was -- there was so far removed from us that no sniper would be able to have them within their reach. I have given my oath here and I'm fully aware of what I'm saying, but I say, upon full responsibility that for as long as I was there in the capacity of a soldier, I never saw a single sniper, never. And I repeat, I say this with full responsibility, I never saw a single sniper there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what were the combat activities between the two warring parties there like, such as the fighting that took place on the 19th of September that we looked at earlier on?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: Observation activities were constant. There were constantly people in the trenches.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, but I rise once again to make submission as to relevance. With few exceptions, the witness's testimony so far has, it seems to me, been dedicated to proving that there was a war on, something that the Prosecution not only does not dispute but because an armed conflict is an element of crimes against humanity, actually affirmatively proved in its own case, so I object to general descriptions of combat activities, general descriptions of army versus army combat. That is not what is alleged in the indictment. General Milosevic is not accused of waging war. He is accused of crimes committed during the waging of war, and for that reason I object to the relevance of the testimony and in particular to the testimony that is called for by the last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Docherty, the Chamber is not with you on this one. Spicasta Stijena is one of the important sites mentioned in the indictment. There are allegations of sniping from that site and the evidence which we have heard has shown that at one time it was held by one party, at another time by another party. This evidence is relevant. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: During active combat activities between the two sides, what level of ammunition would normally be spent by each of the sides?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: To be quite frank, in the beginning the ammunition was spent on a mass scale more out of the intention to intimidate the enemy. As the time went on, however, one realised, to put in that blunt way, that not every bullet hit its target, and the levels of ammunition used were gradually reduced. The army became disciplined. At the very end of the war, the expenditure of ammunition was perhaps at its lowest compared to the beginning of the war. I have already explained that there was no need for to us advance in any way. The Command Staff did not allow for that. However, the opposite side wanted to get hold of an inhabited area or of the road itself. Perhaps an expert would be required now to indicate the implications of a road being captured, where you cut off the only road in the area, you can easily capture the rest of the area. We were, as I already said, firmly set on defending the area, where the other side was firmly set on capturing the area. There was no calm there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. From those positions, Witness, were you at all interested in reaching any part of town under the control of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina or linking up with the part of town under the control of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: I already explained that had we done that, we would have reduced the line of separation, but the superior Command Staff did not allow for this. Since the line of separation was constantly monitored by the SFOR or I don't know what they were called, the international forces at that particular point in time. Perhaps I wasn't clear enough. I can repeat. It was not permitted to change the lines, and I personally did not aspire to anything because I kept to the maxim, I should preserve my own area. My house was behind my back. [Trial Chamber confers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, are you -- have you concluded?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I was thinking of something else, Witness, the weapons that you had, could it reach the positions of the army of Republika Srpska in Grbavica as well as the positions of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and reach as far as Zivalj?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: I understood your question. As for the lines of separation, the weapons had the range of hitting other positions from our positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, just one moment. Let the Judges finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Docherty, I'm still troubled by the objection that you raised, because it appears to us that this is one of the few witness to give evidence that is really relate.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I think there is a misunderstanding, Your Honour, and obviously, I wouldn't have risen if I didn't hold a contrary position to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I think that's understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Because if you look at the first schedule, the incident on the 22nd of November, Sedrenik Street and the incident on the 6th of March, and it is because of the importance of Spicasta Stijena in the indictment that on the on-site visit I think -- I can't remember whether it was the Prosecution or the Defence asked that we visit there, and we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I'm sure it was the Prosecution, Your Honour. I wasn't there but I'm sure it was us. Perhaps this is something I will deal with on cross. I don't understand this witness to be testifying about Spicasta Stijena. I think he is miles out of position. But I think that is not a matter for objection, that's a matter for cross-examination and I intend to take it up there. So that is why I rose. I certainly acknowledge the importance of that geographic feature in our indictment. I don't think he's testifying about that, but that can wait for cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dragas, I just asked you about the weapons that you had and what the range was of the weapons, and what did this firing look like, the firing from these infantry weapons?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: Well, let me say that the range from our position to the positions held by the other side was definitely sufficient. However, but if you look at the map, an inhabited area around the cemetery, for example, I don't know what type of infantry weapons would have the range to hit that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... And where was your position at this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm talking about the position of my unit was from Poljine to the cross roads called Smreka. This is behind Spicasta Stijena, and if you look at Sarajevo from the north to the left and to the right, if I'm facing the town, to the left and to the right is the area of responsibility of my unit that I belonged to. So this area consists of Poljine and the entire line across Poljine. The first populated area is at least two and a half kilometres away, and this area was inhabited by Bosniaks, as they're called now. It's true that there were closer inhabited places, but I'm speaking about a large area that was covered by this unit. The second thing is that certain places --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I see it's not on the transcript. I asked was this area elevated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're asking me about our positions, is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I'm asking the positions, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Our positions were just below the hills of Hum and Grdonj. The line was in a kind of flat area with a mild slope, if I was clear. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do have a photograph here. I don't have the photographs used by the Prosecution, the 360-degree situation, but we do have a photograph P361 which could be more or less useful in order to explain this point that you are now insisting on. And I also wanted to put questions to the witness about that. So we're talking about photograph P361.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not insisting on it. But if you have a photograph that would clarify the matter, let us see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, while we are waiting for the photograph, I think we should ask the witness about who held Spicasta Stijena at the time relevant to this indictment. I understand that Spicasta Stijena did fall under the area of responsibility of your unit, and the report, the combat report which we have been looking at seems to suggest that at least on 18th September 1994, Spicasta Stijena was held by the SRK, that is to say, by forces belonging to your army and probably within your area of responsibility. Now, then it seems to transpire from this document that on the 18th of September, forces of the ABiH tried to occupy Spicasta Stijena and they launched an attack on that day. And by the end of the day they had been able to capture part of Spicasta Stijena and they were able to hold that part until the next morning. Then we don't know what happened except that the report tells us that on the morning, the day after, the SRK started to fiercely shell fire on the captured part of Spicasta Stijena. And then the story ends. But I would like you to give us the ending of the story. What happened? Did Spicasta Stijena then come back, so to say, under your control, or did you lose it? Can you tell us that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I said that we recaptured our original positions in that action. At the beginning it was difficult and later it was easier. When the army of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina was withdrawing, they were routed and they were fleeing, leaving behind weapons and ammunition. As soldiers, you need to understand that. Now it's peace. This is a different country. It's far from the front, far from everything. A soldier who is in war on a daily basis aspires to advance all the time, particularly because Serb property was below and we wanted to shorten that line, but we did not receive the permission for that and we were unhappy about it. But we recaptured the positions that we held up to that day, before we lost them. And then we just stayed there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... The reason why I asked was that when you explained about this the first time, I understood you well, but I wasn't quite sure about whether the area that you talked about in your earlier part of your testimony today was exactly Spicasta Stijena but you have now confirmed this. And can I then just complete my question by asking you about the fort, the old Austro-Hungarian fort. Was that the fort that was just behind, just north of Spicasta Stijena? Because on the site visit when the Chamber visited the area, we did see also the fort, so I was just curious to know whether the fort that you have been talking about was indeed the fort that we saw, which is now ruins, but situated just behind Spicasta Stijena. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's like this. The fort now at the photograph that I see in front of me is located in this corner here. I will indicate that. This part of a wall or this post is now obscuring the fort. This is covering or obscuring the fort. The fort is there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Judge Harhoff, can the witness mark that? He didn't understand whether he was supposed to mark it or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I think he has marked it already.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Spicasta Stijena --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, while we're at it, while we are discussing Spicasta Stijena, I do have another question for you. Where your positions were compared with those of the ABiH, which of those two positions would you say was the highest, giving you a dominating view of the city of Sarajevo, the easiest dominating view?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to give an explanation here, which perhaps will make it understandable for those who did not participate in war. You cannot hold an exposed elevation. It doesn't matter if it is a inhabited area or something else. You cannot be an exposed target. If you want to do something, first of all you have to make sure to protect yourself. So a direct -- so as to be able to prevent a direct incursion into your field of vision and you cannot permit any buildings to be nearby that are obstructing this. If you are exposed -- and can I this on my hand. If there is a trench here on the very boundary, then you are potentially exposed to hits from here, from there. I mean there are 100.000 rifles. One of them is bound to strike you, so who would dare to expose themselves to such an extent and to fire from there? Perhaps they can carry out a reconnaissance clandestinely, but you cannot be exposed. You cannot afford to do that, and everyone is being afraid of being hit, of being shot. I don't know if I answered your question, but I understood you to be asking who was the dominant side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for explaining that. I do understand that it works that way during a war. Still, it was in the interests of each army to be in a dominating position. That would give them a better access to the enemy lines, and that's why I'm asking you. You're telling us that Spicasta Stijena did fall into the hands of the enemy repeatedly. Now, what I want to know is who was initially in the highest position, in the dominating position. I'm happy with your explanation. Still, during an operation like that, you want to be able to profit from your position. I want to know who was in the dominating position. You just told us that the ABiH was trying to retake Spicasta Stijena. That must have been because they thought they could gain something by that. So this brings me back to my first question. Who was in the highest position, who was in the dominating position compared with the other party, a position that they would be able to use and to gain from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand the question. And I will try to provide a detailed answer. If you look at the photograph in front of us, this is the dominant feature in relation to the town. Our positions lay to the right-hand side of this marked -- of this markation of this marking. It wasn't a dominating feature for us. You know why? Because behind this blue line we have our road that we want to maintain. If the enemy should come and capture our positions, then we can no longer put this road to any use. Capturing any part of our positions meant that the road would be lost to us. Now, as for this hill to the left and to the right, this hill had a commanding view of our positions. It was dominant in relation to our positions. We were still able to defend our positions very well because of the distance between our positions and this elevation, if I was clear enough. Behind this hill, there is this slope where you Jagomir lies and the lines were placed the way they were. If you look at the elevation points, this particular elevation point is by far higher than our positions were. Still, as a soldier, I knew this. And some experts would say know this even better than I do. One could never launch an attack from a steep slope. This could never be done. Perhaps this defies logic, but it was always from the foot of the hill that one would be able to capture the hill itself. This was confirmed in several locations during this war. One was at Nisici plateau, for instance. If you're on an elevated feature the enemy can observe and follow every move of yours. If you are positioned well, you still are able to go up the hill and conduct a sabotage action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So what you're trying to tell us is that from the position where you were it would have been difficult to launch an attack, hence, the job of your unit was simply to stay on that hill and not move from there. The whole point of the battle for you was just to stay there. It wasn't to conquer the city of Sarajevo or to fight the other army. That wasn't the point.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, precisely. There's one other point I should like to clarify, if that's of interest to you. This is an excellent photograph, but I can make a drawing of a valley here to the right which -- at the end of which there is a cliff which is the Spicasta Stijena itself. One could approach our positions down this valley. There were two trenches protecting this particular passage between the elevated features. I understand this. No one can claim that there was never such an instance where a person would take a rifle, take a sniper and make his way through to that position and fire. There was no way one could control every single person and their movements and their actions there. But on the basis of my experience, I believe it to be unnatural to expose yourself to show where you are and the moment you fire a weapon from such a vantage point, then you are clearly visible and would be the possible potential victim and one got killed on a daily basis in that war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dragas, I called up this photograph precisely for to you explain this. You mentioned Spicasta just now?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Who was this control of that peak?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: Immediately below the elevation point to the right-hand side were our positions. On the other side, toward the city, facing the city I don't believe there was anyone there. I did not make any attempts at finding out who was at the other end of it. We knew that we dared not go there. Let me show you this location where the fort is. Down below there's a ridge that I was referring to earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you this to clarify the point asked by Judge Mindua. Can you draw for us on this photograph where the trenches or the positions of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina were located?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: This is where the ridge is. And this is where Stijena itself is. Our trench was here. Their trench was there. They kept moving it a bit further up, a bit further down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for His Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. May we have markings to indicate which trench was for the ABiH and which trench is for the Serb army. What markings shall we use? SRK and ABiH?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: We can mark the trenches of the army of the Republika Srpska with two letters, S, or should we use different colours? The trenches of the army of the Republika Srpska should be marked in one colour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: This is the red colour, is it not? As I'm looking at the photograph now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And now the trenches of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: This is Kula or the fort, behind which there is a slope. In blue, I will mark them now. On this hillside there was one trench there. This was as much as one could clearly see.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Where was the line of trenches of your army?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: Let me take the red colour now. And it goes further down.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: On the other side?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: Yes, on the other side toward Jagomir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How far from the peak of the ridge or the summit of the ridge?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: Do you mean how far the fort from that point was? Well, our positions were actually near the fort.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What is the distance between the fort and the ridge?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: I think some 30 --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you draw a red line on the other side of the ridge and write 30 metres? Can you tell us, is that the distance from the summit of the ridge?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, difficult now. He has drawn the line but he is saying that this line was 30 metres long from the summit of the ridge to the other side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now where is the line --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: We have understood that the SRK trenches are not directly visible on this photo and that they are positioned 30 metres behind the ridge that can you see. So you don't need to go further into that. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Any other markings? Because we are at the time when we should have a break. But I would like to finish with this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you marked line with SRK, the red line, that is. And the line marked with 30 metres, can you place the letters SRK there.

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I should like you to put the letters next to where it says 30 metres.

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you mark the blue line with ABH.

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we save this photograph? I have a couple of more questions related to that, but I would not wish to lose this photograph or the markings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, let the photograph be saved. And we'll take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, this photograph should be exhibited, given a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we'll admit this as D256.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The witness is not here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: There is a reason. I had asked for the witness not to be brought in so that I could inform the defence of the response from the registrar to that matter which they raised concerning the use of the office in Sarajevo. I received a reply from the chief of the Victims and Witness Section. I received that on the 21st of June. And I will be making the reply in its entirety available to the Defence. I will just inform the Defence of the -- those paragraphs that appear to me to be most relevant. It says that the VWS provides its support and assistance for the appearance of witnesses before the court in The Hague. Accordingly, for witnesses travelling to The Hague, the operations unit of the VWS would plan and arrange the administrative and logistical requirements of witnesses. Such assistance would be extended to the provision of testimony before the court through videolink. However, with regard to Rule 92 bis witnesses, the VWS does not provide any logistical assistance to the Prosecution or the Defence. Arrangements for the witnesses' transportation for the purpose of certification of their statements are the parties' responsibilities. In fairness to all Defence and Prosecution teams which have not received any logistical assistance from the VWS so far, for the purpose of certifying 92 bis statements, and considering it is critical that the highest levels of integrity and impartiality be maintained in the implementation of the section's policies and procedures, the VWS is not in a position to depart from its policy and make exceptions for a particular party as is now requested by the Defence of Dragomir Milosevic. Those are the relevant paragraphs, and I'll ask the court deputy to transmit this response to the Defence, and to the Prosecution as well. Please let the witness be brought in. Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We have acknowledged the response you have provided, but you didn't say anything about the use of the premises of the ICTY in Sarajevo, the registrar's office. Did you have a response to this, because I would have liked to contact the person in Sarajevo and ask him or her whether our witnesses could use the premises in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's for the -- see, this is a reply from the Victims and Witness Unit. I think they have concerned themselves with the matters that are within their province. I don't believe they can assist in relation to the use of the ICTY. But we did have an indication from Mr. Waespi, did we not, that the Office of the Prosecutor would be prepared to assist in that regard. I don't know whether Mr. Docherty has any information on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I have some information, Your Honour, but I'm not fully involved in this, so I will tell you what I know. I know that Ms. Isailovic and Mr. Hogan have talked about that. I know that Mr. Hogan has made contact with the people in Sarajevo, and they've indicated it would be no problem for the Defence to have an office and office supplies while they're there. I don't know anything beyond that as far as -- I know there were some dates that were possible and some were not possible, but as I say, I'm not fully involved in it so I'm afraid I can't be 100 per cent responsive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic, on this matter, then, you should be in touch, it seems to us, with the Office of the Prosecutor. That is with the -- as far as the use of the office is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just one last point concerning this matter. Mr. Waespi told us last time that as far as the office of the registry is concerned, they can be made entirely available to both parties, i.e., to the defence also, but we didn't get a reply from the registry because we put the question directly to the registry and the registry has not answered. But responded to Mr. Waespi and told him that there are some offices which belong to the registry which we can use whenever we please. We just have to give them our dates. But we didn't get this reply and this is what we haven't had yet, which would be just an acknowledgment of the request we have made. We would just like the registry to confirm this and then we will contact the person whom we are told to contact. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I'll ask the court deputy to see to that. The court deputy will see that it is brought to the attention of the registrar. Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I want to -- I need to correct something I just said. What -- other people, of course, are watching this on the live feed and I'm informed by Mr. Hogan that by an e-mail based on what I think I just said, that the Prosecutor herself has made the decision that OTP is not in a position to provide logistical assistance to Defence lawyers. I can follow up on this. This is a very sparse, bare-bones e-mail, but I of course have just said something quite contrary and I want to make sure that -- let me check into it over the lunch-hour and get a fuller response but I want to correct myself immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you for that information, yes. Let the witness be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have two more photographs to show to the witness, and that will clear up the matter entirely. One of the photographs is 65 ter 03165.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, looking at this photograph, can you tell the Bench whether the name of Spicasta Stijena ever meant anything to you?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: I passed along this route for nine years on my way to school, and I never ever heard it called Spicasta Stijena.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: Immediately behind this hill that we can see here, there's the-- behind the ridge there, there's Andzic Bosko's homestead, and it was during the war that behind the ridges there, the lines were positioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In order for us to be efficient and fast, tell us this: Where were the lines held by the BH army here?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: Behind the ridge there to the right, in the wooded area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please draw the line.

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: Blue, the blue pen?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the blue one will be fine.

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: I'm not as precise as I should like to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Can you please write ABH next to the line.

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Where were your positions?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: You can't see them from here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How far behind the ridge would you say they were?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: Not that far. Depending on the terrain where one could dig trenches. In some places there were rocks and one was unable to dig. But some 15 metres behind the ridge there. I wish to highlight the following. Where you see this peak here, we had our positions behind that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you draw this, please?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: I will. But I will draw an arrow showing the direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But not on this precise spot. It was behind on the slope there.

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: That's precisely what I'm saying. You can't see our positions from here because they were on the other hillside. This is where the ABiH had their trench, and from where they posed a threat to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please mark the location of their trenches in blue.

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: Is this the blue colour now? Can we erase this bit?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you mark the blue marking with letter R.

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And mark a circle there.

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: It seems to be fading out, the colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please save this map as a Defence exhibit, as it is now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be admitted as Exhibit D257.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we show the photograph 65 ter 03322.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. Earlier the witness had said he would use an arrow to indicate the positions of the -- the Serb army, because it couldn't be seen. Has he done that? An arrow to indicate the direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He showed the direction. It can be marked with letters SRK. We have the arrow here. He can place the marking SRK, and it will serve to show that the VRS positions were some 15 metres behind the summit, as he said.

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: If I can repeat this. As far as the ridge is concerned, the slopes were quite steep, and the trenches were positioned where the terrain was more propitious or protective. That's why the lines were some 15 metres behind the summit. So if we had a line going this way, this is where the trenches would say be.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But please mark it with letters SRK.

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: Should I draw what was behind there?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, thank you. Explain to the Judges how far behind the summit the positions were.

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: From the ridge there, there's a gentle slope going down to what seems like a bed or a trough and trenches were some 10 to 15 metres away from the ridge. The objective was to observe the entrance to where we have the letter R in blue, because it was at that point where one could leave the trenches and launch an attack with a view to capturing the entire area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please mark this -- this wedge cutting across the ridge in blue -- in the blue pen.

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: That will be it roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In line 12, it says the entire area where, as the witness was saying that this was a good vantage point from where the road could be attacked. Is that right, witness?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: Yes, to attack the road or the general area, because around the road you have inhabited areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have the photograph thus marked, given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be D258.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tapuskovic. Witness, this hill, could you give us a name of this hill, please? I'm putting the question to you because in the transcript on page 36 on line 17 -- line 19, rather, you said that you'd never heard of Spicasta Stijena. Is that right? Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you understood me correctly. This area is called Smreka. The wedge, which was basically a pedestrian track to the town itself, is called Okuke. You can see it behind the tree on the left-hand side on the photograph. That's where the water reservoir for the town is located now. At the time I went to school, there was no water reservoir there and it was called Krivi Kamen. It was a rock that we would use as a bench to rest as we would be on our way to school.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, what is Spicasta Stijena?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That probably relates to this ridge, the whole length of the ridge. Below the ridge there's a road going to the right, and that's where the roads meet. This is what we call the cross roads, this place. And that's where Bosko's house is nearby. I never heard of that place name, Spicasta Stijena. In our language, "spic" means summit or peak, whereas the whole geographic feature, the higher ground is a ridge, quite a steep one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To follow up on Judge Mindua's question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The ridge, as we see it in this photograph, were there any fighters of yours there or those of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: Not on the ridge itself. I have tried to explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have already admitted this photograph as Defence exhibit. Can we show the photograph 65 ter 03322.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, what it that we see here? We can see a car. Can you please explain for us?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: I have to get my bearings first.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I can tell you that I received the photograph from the Prosecution. Can you orient yourself?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: What can we see from this vantage point. We can see Zlatiste.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is that the road you were protecting or not?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: No, that's not the one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us something concerning the events transpiring in the summer of 1995: Did you experience anything in particular at the time and what was that period like, the months of June, July and August.

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: Let's keep the photograph here. I might even remember what this shows. At the time the fighting, or rather, the combat activities launched by the BH army grew in intensity. My unit was providing assistance to the units placed at Nisici plateau. I spent my time there from mid-June or perhaps from 10 June onwards. There was fierce terrible fighting. We were astonished to see the extent of ammunition used by them. The positions we held at Mali Jasen were practically razed to the ground. We will no artillery support whatsoever. We mounted as much defence as we could. There were six dead and 12 wounded in my part of the positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you were astonished to see the amounts of ammunition. Whose ammunition?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: The BH army's, and I'm referring to artillery pieces. They were launching attacks from us from the direction of Korita, which is an inhabited area that can easily be reached from Breza and Vares. They kept mounting attacks against us. Then they even captured two of our trenches. We were able to recapture the trenches the following day and we did not suffer anymore losses. The situation became more stable.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, we're running out of time. I have to be quick. How long did this fighting last involving those quantities of ammunition?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: Four to five days.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And later on?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: I left the positions later and I went back home, and a shell landed at my house and wounded me. I have the records about that and I can provide you with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Dragas. Mr. Dragas my name is John Docherty. I'm one of the prosecuting attorneys on this case. I have some questions for you this morning. And if at any time any of my questions are not clear, please ask me to clear it up before you try and answer, so that you and I keep communicating and don't get into confusion. Is that all right, sir?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: Yes, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I want to begin, sir, talking about the testimony you've given concerning your positions and concerning the high ground. I'm going to be showing you some maps, I'm going to be showing some photographs and this may take a little while, but I think the geography is important to clear up. Could we begin, please, by seeing Defence Exhibit 255. Mr. Dragas, on the monitor in front of you is the map that you marked earlier this morning when Mr. Tapuskovic was asking you some questions. And the letter K on there, that marks the position of your house. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: Yes. That's the house after 1967. And it is still there to this date.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And then there's a line. And you said that is the line -- the road that you used to take when you were going to school. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: Yes. But until 1967.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Okay. And when you marked that, talking about going to school, you said that that walk to and from school every day for nine years was what gave you the familiarity you have got with the geography of this area. Do you remember saying that, or words to that effect?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: Well, I got to know this terrain in detail. I could now give you the names of the streets where I walked Sedrenik, Malta Podruk, Kriva street.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I'm sure you could, but I'm just asking if this is the way that you got your familiarity, living there, walking two and from school.

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And was it, or did I mishear, in connection with your walk to and from school, that you first mentioned Sharpstone, or Spicasta Stijena?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you the term. Spicasta Stijena is a term that I had not heard before the war or even after the war. This area where we walked by, we called it Smreka, and Raskirsa was even closer to where we were walking. This is where two roads met. We always took the shorter road down at Okuke to Krivi Kamen and then towards Malta and on to school.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. Dragas, I apologise for interrupting but let me just -- I need to jump in at this point. What I'm asking is when you first heard the term sharp -- in English Sharpstone or in your language Spicasta Stijena, and I really appreciate that you've got a good memory and that you know the routes that you took very, very well. But the question I'm asking is where you first heard that term, and I believe you have said you did not hear it until at least the war and maybe not even then. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: Yes, that is entirely correct. Because, sir, in our language, the word "spic," it refers -- it may refer to something like the point of a pencil, something that is sharp that has a peak, and this here is not a peak. It's a ridge. So quite naturally, the word Spicasta Stijena was not used. That would be my assumption. I don't know. Somebody called it Spicasta Stijena, probably somebody who doesn't really know what the word "spic" means as opposed to "ridge." All place names here are called -- you use the term strana, slope, if there is a slope or "vrh," summit, if there is a summit. So you always follow the natural phenomenon when you name a place.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. Dragas, I'm sorry. I really have to ask to you limit yourself to asking the questions. There is a limited amount of time. There is a fair amount to cover. I appreciate that you often have more to say. I understand that, but I'm really just trying to get out the points that are important and the points that are relevant. On the map in front of you, Exhibit 255 there is a small circle marked with the letter B. Is this the fort? Did you mark the forth with the letter B?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: Well, that would correspond to the site where the fort was. Letter B marks the location of Bosko's house and the fort is this here. The point that we didn't mark. And could you just wait for just a moment, let me concentrate and look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And I know you said when Mr. Tapuskovic was asking questions that the map is hard to read, between the fine print on the map and your eyesight. Why don't we do this. Let's look at a photograph of the fort and make sure that you and I are talking about the same fort.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: So could we please see 65 ter 03323.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. Dragas, is that the fort that you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: Yes, that's the fort.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: All right. And now if we could go back to Defence Exhibit 255, please. And while we're waiting for the map, Mr. Dragas, have you ever heard that fort called the name Mala Kula?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: Yes. Before the war, Magra's company had their stores there for the shop before the war. There was a guard there and then the stuff was brought there and taken away. I don't know. I wasn't there but I know that it was used for this purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, on this map that's in front of you, do you see the letter -- just yes or no, do you see the dot marked with the letter B?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And isn't Mala Kula, the fort that we've been talking about and the photograph you just looked at, to the right of that letter B quite some distance, about where the confrontation lines start to turn to the south. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: I don't think so. This is where the fort is, and do you know why I'm saying this? I will give you an answer. This line goes right to the big fort and then it goes down to a location called Tenerovica [phoen] and then it goes up slightly and goes on to Donje Pjesajic and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. Dragas, are you familiar with a neighbourhood in Sarajevo called Sedrenik?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: Yes. I passed through it on my way to school.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Sedrenik is in the north-east area of the city. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And have you had an opportunity, Mr. Dragas, to look at the amended indictment in this case?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: So you're not aware that there are several instances of sniping that are alleged in Sedrenik?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the question is: Did you see the amended indictment? How could the witness say anything about any indictment? And what could the question about an amended indictment mean anything to a witness like this? Amended indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: He answered no. So we move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I need to use a document that is not on the list in order to try and clear this up.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
