utterances.text: I want to show the witness the cover screen, if you will, to the collection of 360-degree panoramic videos. It's a map of the city of Sarajevo onto which have been superimposed the locations, as the Prosecution alleges, of the various sniping incidents. I want to display that map to him and just point out where these Sedrenik sniping incidents are alleged to have occurred

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We're waiting on a map to be --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Oh, I was waiting on a ruling that it was allowed. So we can stop waiting for each other, and Ms. Bosnjakovic, could we see the map, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. Dragas, I'll direct your attention to the three numbers in the upper right-hand corner of this map. The numbers are, from left to right, 15, 7 and 10 and once you have looked at those and once you've got your bearings, the question I've got is are those number in the area of Sarajevo called Sedrenik? And just take the time you need to look at the map and ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, since this map contains markings that we have not yet seen at all, we don't know what it is. We have not been in a situation to verify what the markings mean and we haven't been able to investigate it. And since this has been such a major point of late, what time does this map refer to and when was this map made. We don't know anything, and now we have a situation where the witness is supposed to answer a question. This was not on the list at all. We -- in principle, if this had been put on the list yesterday, we might have been able to do something about it or, rather, today, but it hasn't, so I don't know what this map represents, when this map was made and what does it have to do with what this witness is talking about? What time does it refer to? Who made the markings?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you objecting to the map being shown because it wasn't on the list, or are you merely asking for more background information about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we're simply asking for some additional information so that we know what this is all about and what time this refers to, who made the markings. What is this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour, this map was given to the Defence months ago. This, when you open up the DVD containing the 360s, this is the first thing you see, and you click on these numbers in order to get to the 360 of the particular shelling or sniping incident. The map was made by the Office of the Prosecutor using the map that has, I think it is the one that is used in evidence quite a bit but zoomed back considerably, and the markings were put there by us. As for the date of the map, I'm not entirely sure why that matters. I don't know that Sedrenik can be said to have moved. And really the question -- the dates -- the relevant dates would be the dates of the incidents in question, and as I say, you click on any -- not on this version because this is a screen capture, but on the DVD version you click on these to see the sniping incidents, so because there is some issue about where this fort is and where Sharpstone was, I thought that we could show this to the witness and have him say yes or no that those three incidents, which ones we allege occurred in Sedrenik, Mrs. Selmanovic, Ms. Dedovic, and Mr. Zunic, that those are indeed in Sedrenik. That's the only purpose behind displaying this to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, evidently you have been in possession of the map for some time and the background information has been provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it is possible that we had it in our possession. I don't want to deny that at this point, but I have never as a Defence counsel used any of the maps that I marked and I never exhibited it in court. I think that this is not an entirely fair procedure, and I don't think that I can testify and I don't think that I can I make any markings on any maps or anything. This is something that the Prosecution produced in the course of its work, but I could have produced any number of such maps. I could have marked any number of such maps and I could have presented them as the way I see things, and this doesn't mean a thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Docherty, will you be relying on the markings on the map?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I'm just asking the witness if those markings are in Sedrenik. That's -- when he answers that question yes or no, the map goes away. I'm not introducing the map.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as far as I'm able to see, this is Sedrenik, in my opinion. Because to the right of number 10 here, it should be the road. And then further away to the right there should be this place known as Kamenjara, below the Seven Woods, Sedam Suma. I assume that based on all this, this is Sedrenik. It's not really quite clear but if I really had to tell you whether it is or it isn't, then I tell you that it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I absolutely believe that this question to be admissible, had the witness been shown an unmarked map and to indicate where Sedrenik is. And I'm sure that he would have been able to do so. But a map that has certain markings made by a party to the proceeding is, I think, not proper. I'm sure that this witness can tell you where Sedrenik is because he has lived there all his life.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The question may be put and the witness may answer it. Indeed, I think he has already given an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And at this time, we can take the map away. Thank you. And could we see -- thank you -- D255 again.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Dragas, all I can really do is ask you, having seen that map with the three numbers on it, are you sure that you've got that fort in the right place? And I think you indicated that this letter B and the open circle is actually the home of someone whose name begins with the letter B. Let me ask you this: Would you please, with the blue pen so we know whose markings are whose, put a mark where the fort, Mala Kula in the photograph you saw a little while ago is. And just take your time, and if you need this blown up more, we can do that, because we won't lose the markings since this is already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you please zoom in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Witness, just a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witness concentrated very hard when the Prosecutor asked him about this spot that he marked with B, and in the end he did say what it is. He gave his definitive answer. He did mention a house, but in the end he did explain what it was that he marked with letter B. And he explained that there was a house there too, but, first of all, he marked that location and also indicated there was a house, telling us who the owner of the house was, but he didn't change his mind as to what it was that he actually marked with letter B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What's your point? I don't understand the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution is insinuating that this spot marked with letter B is the house owned by someone whose name is Boskovic -- or rather Bosko. Bosko's house. He mentioned Bosko's house.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Bosko Andzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I don't want to ask any further questions. Perhaps he can explain what it was that he marked with letter B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, can you mark where the fort -- fort was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I'm able to orient myself on this map, which is quite unclear to me and I can't really see very clearly the markings here, it says Kosevo and then I can't see anything, I can't see anything. It is not really very clear. So I am unable to orient myself. But if I really had to tell you, that would be the fort. Perhaps if we could just move -- move it to the right -- just -- okay. That would be, I think, more accurate than it was just a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. Dragas, you said that the map is difficult to read and also indicated that you're having some trouble seeing it. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Then I tell you what. Let's look at some photographs instead. And let's look at -- we'll first look at D256 and then in a few minutes we'll look at D258.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Oh, and before we do that, for the sake of completeness, I'll tender this, for what it's worth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P781, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. Dragas, do you see the photograph on the monitor now?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And don't worry, I'm not going to ask for any markings on this one. But, you indicated in your direct testimony - correct me if I'm wrong - that your position would be about a kilometre further to the left of this picture, is that correct, your position, that is, in Pionirska Dolina?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And that would be one kilometre from the left margin of this photograph. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Now, is the fort known as Mala Kula behind the hill at any point on the photograph that's in front of us now?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I understand what you're asking me about.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Well, then let me clear it up before we go on. You did the best you could with the map, Defence Exhibit 255, but it was difficult, the map was hard to read. So I thought it might be helpful to figure out where the fort was, in your mind, to use some photographs instead. I understand the fort not to be visible itself in any of these straight-on photographs, because it's a little bit over the hill, on the other side, if you will. And so I'm going to start with this photograph and then we'll go to a photograph that is farther to the right, and I'm just going ask you, over the ridge at what point you would find the fort of Mala Kula. Is on this photograph at all, and if it is, can you just tell us where?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: If you followed what I was saying well --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Dragas. I think you got out the words: "If you followed what I was saying well," and then I stopped you.

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: In this blue rectangle, in the part of the photograph where we see this curtain, that's what the position of Mala Kula would be. That's where it would stand on the hill if our view was not obstructed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: All right. And now, at the risk of beating a dead horse, I'm going ask for D255 one last time. Now on your direct testimony, Mr. Dragas, you indicated that your position in the trench was about 100 metres in front of your house. That's the --

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your house is marked with a K?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And there's ten times 100 metres in a kilometre, correct, a thousand metres?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And so isn't that fort farther to the right than you originally indicated? Because on this map, I put it to you, that fort is not a kilometre or more from your positions, since you said that your positions were a kilometre from the left-hand margin of the photograph we were just looking at. And I'm just asking you -- this isn't a test. I'm just asking you isn't it probable that that fort is quite farther off to the right, based on the photograph you just looked at?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: Let me look at it so that I can focus on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Take the time you need.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Those who have this interest, the break will be from 12.30 until 1.30 for lunch.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Do you need more time, Mr. Dragas?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: Is it possible that the fort, as we can see it on this scale of the map, some ten millimetres further to the right but not more than that. It's roughly the right position of the fort, if I'm able to read correctly the map. And this road toward Gornji Mrkovici and Cavljak, Kukrike, Donji Mrkovici, and Nahorevo further on. I suppose that I marked its position well. Perhaps it also should be positioned several -- a centimetre to the right. And if you allow this correction, my house may well have been 130 metres away from the trenches. I never measured the distance. The fort may have been some 850 metres away. I'm not a surveyor. I'm speaking as far as I'm able to estimate the distances. I know for a fact that from Bascarsija to my native home in Mrkovici, the distance was --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness repeat the distance, how many kilometres?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: How far was it from Bascarsija to your home in Mrkovici one more time? The interpreter did not hear that.

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: The distance between Bascarsija and my home in Mrkovici was 11 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: It is possible to measure it now, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And thank you, Mr. Dragas. I appreciate -- we spent a lot of time on that. I appreciate your patience. I'm going to move to a different topic now, and I'm going to go back to -- with Defence Exhibit 258, talk about the position of the front lines on the hill that we can see in Defence Exhibit 258, which is another photograph. And while we wait for that, Mr. Dragas -- there it is. While you were in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, did you know an operations officer with the rank of major called Veljevic?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: I didn't. The family name seems to ring a bell, but, hmm, as an officer, hmm, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: All right. Now on this Defence Exhibit 258 we see the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina's trench lines in blue. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And your testimony is that if we walk up and over the hill and down the other side, in about 15 metres we would come to the trenches of the army of the Republika Srpska. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And as a soldier with experience in this area, would you agree with me that it would be a fairly simple matter for a soldier or a sniper in the Republika Srpska trenches to walk that 15 metres and take a shot into the area of the houses that we see at the, say the bottom third of the screen?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with you. I'm speaking from personal knowledge. I would not expose myself to such danger, because if you look at the blue line and if you show up there, you're a potential target to anyone from the general area. You wouldn't be protected there. I myself would not dare do that, which doesn't mean that I'm claiming that there weren't such isolated cases of people going into such forays. But can I tell that you I have children and I'm a religious person, and can I swear that I saw at least ten civilians, Muslims in front of my lines felling trees. And I wouldn't ever wish to harm any single of them and I did not even warn them to move away, because I know how difficult it would have been for me if I had to get some fuel wood for me and my children, and I spoke about this with my father, who said to me, Son, you should never do to others what you do not wish to be done to yourself. I can, however, tell you that such escapades would indeed have been very dangerous.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: And I mean to walk up the ridge and become a possible target.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness. Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: While we're talking about exposing one's self, take a look at the blue line, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina trenches. They're quite a bit lower -- they're low down on the hill, is that correct? Is that a fair way of characterising their location?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And to get to a higher position, whoever is in those trenches would themselves have to walk out and expose themselves, isn't that correct, to fire from you and your colleagues, your comrades. In other words, to move up that hill?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. But in the left-hand corner of the map you have the positions of the BH army trenches or did I say on the right-hand side? No. I'm correcting myself. On the left-hand hand. These two blue lines represent the trenches of the BH army. They were the potential danger for the trenches of the army of the Republika Srpska there. For this reason, a curtain was put up and barricades were erected to obstruct the line of sight. We were waging the war within our possibilities and tried to survive as best we could.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to get back again to Mr. Veljevic, who I mentioned a couple of moments ago, because he when he testified was asked also to mark these trenches and the different lines, and I'd like to show you now the results of that work.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: If we could please see Prosecution Exhibit 743.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have to say that some important matters said by the witness were not entered into the transcript in the English language. Or were entered with a different meaning and whatever was of capital importance was not entered into the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We haven't got a lot of time. Perhaps if we could adjust the English translation from lines 4 to 13, going back to what the witness said in B/C/S. It is my impression that entire sentences are left out. So it seems to me that he is talking slowly enough and clearly enough, so surely, a better translation could have been given, and that way, have a transcript of everything that he said, because to be honest, half of the sentences are missing. There's entire passages left out. For example, the explanation of those trenches is very interesting and there's a whole sentence left out there and explanation. If you read the English it is -- it doesn't make any sense. It is illogical, whereas in B/C/S it made perfect sense and it was very well explained the way those trenches worked. So, if you don't mind, I think that perhaps after the hearing we could adjust the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, do you remember the answer that you gave? Because if you do, I would ask to you repeat it so that we can have it in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what was unclear. Perhaps I should be told.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps we could ask him to repeat precisely what he said about corners. It seems there was another picture. He said something about a left-hand corner and he was explaining what was going on in the left-hand corner versus what was going on in the trenches held by the army of the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What was the question that you asked?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I don't remember, Your Honour. I'll need to look at the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Let me help you out. The question put to the witness on page 59, line 2, read as follows: "And to get to a higher position, whoever is in those trenches would themselves have to walk out and expose themselves, isn't that correct, to fire from you on your -- to fire from you on your colleagues, your comrades, in other words, to move up that hill. Such reads the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So that's the question and it is the answer to that that Ms. Isailovic says has not been fully reflected in the transcript. But I see Mr. Tapuskovic has a suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What the witness said was a very direct explanation of how the trenches were positioned to the left-hand side and all the other sides and what one could see from the trenches that the BH army held in the left-hand corner. What he said about that problem, what -- from those trenches up there toward the ridge was that one could see what he said one could see and we don't have that in the transcript at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Docherty, this is a technical matter and also a question of -- of fairness, and the Chamber's been trying to arrive at the best position to resolve this issue. Ms. Isailovic, you had suggested that we might have the -- have a record of actually what the witness said and have that translated and presented to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. That would seem the most reasonable thing to do. It would avoid wasting time and, anyway, he wouldn't probably be able to repeat exactly what he said. He would be using different words, anyway, so that is not something that we could fairly ask a human being to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: There is apparently a procedure to -- to have a transcript verified if a party requests verification a procedure has been elaborated and I'll just ask the court deputy to be in touch with Ms. Isailovic. You have to identify the particular passage. CLSS will provide the translation. So let us proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Hello again, Mr. Dragas. On the screen in front of you there is a photograph. This is it the markings that were made by witness Veljevic when he was asked about the trench lines, the very same photograph you were shown and I take it you don't agree with him and the ABH there could mean that the ABH trenches were also over the ridge. But that's not your testimony, is it.

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: No. This was arbitrarily drawn. This photograph provides a much better view than the other one. The trenches go exactly here. This is where Okuke is and that's where the road is up there. And now the trenches run below this and that's where the entranceway to Bosko's house is, and behind there is the large fort and the road through the seven woods and that's where the crossroads is. So they are positioned logically because trenches cannot be placed in a way which is not logical. Otherwise, they are not sustainable and they cannot prevent the enemy from advancing. That's according to the tactics of warfare.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic. Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... Not intervene. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: That was a very long answer, Mr. Dragas, but to boil it down, no, you don't agree with this photograph, do you? And please, yes or no.

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: Not fully, I don't agree fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: The photograph you drew was quite -- the markings you made on the photograph were quite different, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I want to talk with you just of two topics left, I think. This probably unfortunately will carry over until after the break but not very long. We were talking -- you were talking with Mr. Tapuskovic about the ABiH army's attack on the 18th or 19th of September 1994. Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: You talked there?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't mean to interrupt. But you talked there about a fort. Was the fort that you were talking about there Mala Kula?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Now I'd like to take a look at the exhibited -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I just need one moment, I've gotten lost in my notes. But I'm looking for the combat report from the ABiH that was displayed to the witness, the one that was signed by Mr. -- General Karavelic. And I think it is DD00 -- it's Defence Exhibit 156. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Now, on the left-hand side, Mr. Dragas, you see the English translation. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: Probably. I don't understand English.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And you see that, for example, at one point there are three lines on the page rather than text. Do you see the place that I'm referring to? Where things have not --

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Where things have not been translated.

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Now if we could scroll down the English, please. There's this area "our forces," and that has been translated. And now if we could please go to page 2 in both English and B/C/S. And we see once again there is a portion of this document that has not been translated into English. I'm going, because I think it important, to put it into evidence in English, I'm going to ask you to read a part of this, so if the upper third of the B/C/S document could be expanded, please. And I'm going to give you two benchmarks here, Mr. Dragas. I'm going to ask to you start reading right at the beginning and then look at the bottom of the first chunk of text, and do you see the name Cosovic Adnan, 15th MTBR, which I presume means mountain brigade. Do you see that name?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to read, sir, in your language, and slowly so that the interpreters can interpret it, what is said between the beginning of this page and the name Cosovic Adnan, 15 MTBR, the portion that was not translated into English. And before we do that, I will point out that the -- the translation here indicates it was done in Belgrade and not by CLSS, not, in other words, by the OTP. Mr. Dragas, would you begin reading, please?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: "During the night, the captured part could not be fortified because of open space, open or exposed space and because it was impossible to do any works. Due to losses suffered, the units retreated to the initial LO," probably initial positions. "In the course of the attack, the following losses were suffered due to artillery -- intensive artillery fire. There were three dead, two from 120th Mountain Brigade, one from MUP, there were 26 wounded, 15 from 120th Mountain Brigade, six from the MUP and five from 105th Motorised Brigade," I take it. "Fighter Nusret Kalabusic was seriously wounded from a sniper who is a member of the second 'V,' ATBR Brijesce. In the area of Curine Njive, Trebevic, fighter Adnan Cosovic from the 15th Motorised Brigade was wounded."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: What this says, then, Mr. Dragas, is that the ABiH was driven back to their starting lines because of intense SRK artillery fire. Is that what the document says?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: That's what it says. But let me draw your attention to one illogical matter as a person and as a soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Excuse me. And the ABiH went back to their initial positions, according to the document; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: Yes. But the report indicates --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. Dragas --

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: -- wounded from a sniper in Trebevic. That's impossible. No weapon can have that range.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Okay. But what I wanted to talk to you about is that the reference here is to artillery weapons. You testified that your unit had automatic and semi-automatic rifles. We have here a number of wounded soldiers, 15 from one brigade alone, and the reference is to artillery, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: It says here that it was due to artillery fire. However --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Did you --

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: -- I don't think that this was the ratio of -- or the balance of forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Did you at your positions -- you've testified that you had automatic and semi-automatic rifles. Did you not also have mortars, 82-millimetre mortars, at least?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: There weren't any in my unit. Probably the commanding officers of higher ranks knew this. There were such weapons in the army of the Republika Srpska. However, I state that from the beginning of the war until the 17th of January, 1996, I was never absent from the territory of my municipality and I managed to save my skin on the 15th of January, 1996 by finding refuge in Ruda. You have to know that I did not investigate or make inquiries about other matters. My area of movement was between my home and my trenches.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. At this stage we have to break. We'll break for one hour. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.30 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We will take the next break at 3.35 and will endeavour to finish at about 4.25 or 4.30., if that's possible, yes. Mr. Docherty, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour, as the first item of business, before lunch, I had shown the witness 65 ter number 03323. It was a photograph of the fort. I didn't tender it at the time. I've changed my mind, and at this time I would tender that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P782, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. Dragas, I just have a few more questions for you. One question before I start my next topic. You mentioned the weapons that you an your comrades had at your positions. You described them as infantry weapons, rifles and so forth. Did you have in your unit M84 machine-guns?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: I really cannot be sure. We did have the M53s, and I didn't see it, but I think that there were one or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Okay. And the M84 is a more recent version of the M53. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: Probably. I -- it's a lighter machine-gun than the other one. Probably has the same characteristics as the M53, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Now, the last topic I want to cover with you, Mr. Dragas, and then I will be done, would you tell the Chamber what you mean by the term "drawing room general"?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: In your direct testimony when Mr. Tapuskovic was asking --

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: I did remember saying that sentence, "drawing room general." Yes. This was kind of jargon among the soldiers. A general that we would never see, who was formally a general and you know that he exists. It's somebody who is probably sitting somewhere in the warm, dry, with furniture, but this does not refer to the general on whose behalf I'm testifying now. He was very disciplined. He toured the positions of the soldiers. He had empathy for their problems. He convinced them that what we were doing was very right, There was no need to abuse the command or senior officers, that there would should be respect and discipline.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: He had -- I'm sorry, I just wanted to finish. He had a realistic approach or attitudes towards people, towards civilians. Anything that was before him, he didn't spare himself. He would go out in the rain, in the dark. He had an old vehicle with a bumpy road just like the rest of us. He never complained and I believe, you know, that I have no objections or anything to say against him and the way he waged war, based on his training. At any point in time, he was communicating with people and you could see his character and his ethics in the communication with these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: You were a private soldier on the front line. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And how often, how frequently, did you see General Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: I cannot say that now, was I really wasn't keeping a record. But something that did stick to my mind when I did see him was at the hospital, then also at the small fort, and at one time we met on the road above Poljine. That is exactly where the municipality of Vogosca and Centar border on each other. I don't know. Perhaps there were other occasions sometime during 1994 and 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And in those meetings, when General Milosevic would come to the lines, he was learning things. He was learning what the soldiers' problems were, he was learning what the ammunition and the food situation were. Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: General Milosevic was a man who take care, in your view, to be well-informed and to understand what was happening with the troops under his command. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: While you were serving with the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, did you hear allegations, either face to face or through the media, of crimes being committed by the Bosnian Serb army or by the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: We, the regular soldiers, didn't have an opportunity to get reports like that. It's true that we had company meetings, not that often, but these meetings were held in order to say that ammunition should not be spent just like that, that we should save or resources and not to violate discipline. That we shouldn't do anything that is outside of the bounds of what is permissible. If there was a truce, then there should be a truce. Nobody could do anything on their own initiative. A couple of times, I was a witness when one of ours perhaps by accident fired a bullet. The police would come and get him and they would have to say why they did it, so if you're not under threat you cannot fire, and truce must -- a truce must be respected. That's the gist of it. What I'm saying is that we didn't have the kind of information so that we could judge whether something was proper and correct, so I really don't have the right perhaps training or information in order to be able to judge whether something was done properly or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: If there were allegations that the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps was committing atrocities, would you expect a well-informed commanding officer, like Dragomir Milosevic to be aware that these allegations were being made in the press, for example, on the television?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question? I understood everything except I wasn't sure how it goes on from well-informed general.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: You have testified that Dragomir Milosevic, in your opinion, was a general who took care to keep himself well-informed about what was going on in his command, and from that, the question that I have is: If there were allegations, for example, on the television news, in the international press, by human rights organisations, by any source that the Bosnian Serb army was committing atrocities or war crimes, would you not except a commanding general who was as well-informed as Dragomir Milosevic to be aware that these allegations were being made about his troops?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: Well, all of this needs to be explained. I said that the general tried to be well-informed at firsthand. I don't know if he did that -- I mean, you would need to ask that of him, whether he did that because he didn't believe those who reported back to him and he felt like he needed to check back, which is logical to me. Perhaps he wanted to know everything that was going on. All kinds of misinformation is disseminated an untruths during the war, so he wanted to make sure if something was true. If it wasn't true, I assume, or if it was true, I assume the general would have reacted because, as I said, when we asked -- when we retook the small fort, our way was open towards the town, towards the State Hospital of Kosevo. And if we did that, we would have shortened our lines. We would have destroyed the sniper nests which destroyed Radomir Gajic, Nedzo Grujic, Novo Neskovic, Janju Dzokic, Saju Simeonovic. These are the names that I remember right now, but I could give you more names. All the territories where they were passing were protected but a wind could move the blanket. Somebody would appear and then they would end up being the victim, and he said, No, we will live the way we have been living so far, you can fortify where you are and take your military assignments seriously. There will be no further advance, the war will end, and then we will see what is ours and what is not and higher powers will decide that. Now what I want to say is this. The general, as far as I know him, I would believe that he would react and intervene. Another thing: I believe that if the general were to feel guilty, he would not have come to The Hague so easily. You can see that many people are in hiding.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Dragas, as you said in your answer, which was quite long, and with respect, I don't think responded to my question. You said that there is always sorts of misinformation in war. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Commanding officer checks those things out, doesn't he?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will be very brief. Just a few clarifications.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You talked about this event over the two days, 19th of September, 1994, before the events occurred in the summer of 1995, can you please tell us how many similar actions of this kind took place, such as the one described in the Defence document D156?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: Similar events of higher or lower intensity were numerous. Perhaps there were 38 active, very active attacks on our lines throughout the war. If you calculate that, it turns out to be about ten or 11 per year.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: With the main objective as what?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: The objective was to break through the lines to capture the road. Well, so that you can understand me, there was Juka Prazina, his uncle, the so-called Amidza.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, there is no need to go into that. Just tell me, what would have happened had the road at that place where you were in front of your house, what would have happened then with the positions where you were, you soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ANDELKO DRAGAS
utterances.text: We would have been completely captured.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness. That concludes your evidence. Thank you for giving it, and you may now leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You recall that I had asked the court deputy to be in touch with the registry about the matter raised by the Defence. I will ask him to provide the information that he has received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. During lunch break I spoke with the acting chief of CMSS, who confirmed that the Sarajevo and Belgrade field offices are indeed the property of the OTP, and therefore the facilities would say not be able to be made available to the Defence for the taking of witness statements. However, there may be a possibility of using the facilities for certifying those statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. The next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not getting any translation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters apologise. Could the counsel repeat what he said? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's document DD00-3985, and it contains the basic information for the next witness, T-48, which has protective measures in the form of a pseudonym and face distortion. And can we please show this ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please be seated. And you may begin, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document identifying the witness should be admitted under seal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let it be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will become D259, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now can we please move into private session so that I could inform the Chamber about this witness's particulars.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness T-48, can you please, in the briefest way, tell us something about what was happening at the beginning of the events in 1992, in the briefest possible way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-48
utterances.text: In 1992, the war was going on in Croatia. Already there was some changes in Bosnia and Herzegovina. In the beginning, these were minor incidents, provocations at work and traffic, and things like that and then after the killing at the wedding in Sarajevo, things escalated. After that, people self-organised in the local communes and in the neighbourhoods where they lived. In the beginning, these were joint guard duties of people in the areas where they lived. This was the case in the Nedzarici settlement in Novi Grad municipality in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please stand up and point out on this map for the Judges why Nedzarici is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-48
utterances.text: Yes, very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Just to ensure that the -- that his image will not be broadcast. I understand he has image distortion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Is that being attended to? Yes, it is being attended to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You can go back to your seat. And what happened, if you could go quickly over what happened in relation to the following events, if you can do it quickly and just point to the most important events.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-48
utterances.text: At the beginning, the people didn't expect that the conflicts would escalate. There were even some agreements among local communes where the majority populations were of different ethnic backgrounds or mixed. But in the settlement where I lived on the 14th of May, in the morning, at dawn, well-armed well-equipped forces wearing black overalls, people who were not from those areas, they were not locals and they were not part to those agreements about the maintenance of peace and good neighbourly relations. And escorted, to be quite specific, in front of the place where I lived, escorted by an armoured personnel carrier ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you don't have to go that slow. You can talk a little bit faster.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-48
utterances.text: They tried to take this neighbourhood. The neighbourhood that I'm talking about, Nedzarici, covers an area of about one square kilometres. There are about 700 families living there, maybe 2, 3.000 people living there, and the ethnic background of those people, most of them are Serbs. After this attack, we managed to defend ourselves, and from that time on, the war in the proper sense of the word started.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now can you tell me what does the position of Nedzarici look like?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-48
utterances.text: The entire neighbourhood is in a very unenviable position, because on the one hand, you have Dobrinja 5, these are high-rise buildings, apartment buildings, and then there is the Mojmilo neighbourhood, then the Mojmilo hill, then Alipasino Polje where the buildings, some buildings are up to 18 storeys high. And then further down to Stup, there's the refrigerator facility, the fire-fighting facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. Could you please explain Stup, Hladnica refrigerator facility, and a fire-fighting column -- Gazni Stup, what are those buildings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-48
utterances.text: Well, these are high-rise buildings, buildings that dominate this wider area and they used this higher ground to fire on the population, on the positions, on the troops, on the moving vehicles and so on. Nedzarici, you mostly have family house one to two storeys high.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what other geographical points can you perhaps point to up in the north?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-48
utterances.text: Well, as far as the encirclement goes, here you have Zuc, Sokolje, Hum and then to the other side, Hrasnica, Mount Igman that dominates the whole area. It is a high mountain.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please, could you please approach the map, and mark the highest summits on Mount Igman at Hrasnica and point them out to the Judges and tell us quite clearly what the elevations are. You can -- you can just get up with the earphones and then I will put the microphone closer to you. Could you remember and then you could tell us later?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-48
utterances.text: Crni Vrh elevation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How high is it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-48
utterances.text: 1.504 metres. That is the highest summit on Mount Igman that dominates Igman, and the broader area Ilidza, Nedzarici, Blazuj.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please indicate at least two other summits there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-48
utterances.text: Obesenjak, 1.240 metres. It is even closer to this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And is there in this red circle an elevation that is marked somewhere on this boundary, the confrontation line? Further up to the north.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-48
utterances.text: Yes. There's Radzin Vrat, 1.400 -- 1.480 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is that at Hrasnica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-48
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And could you now tell the Judges as you told us, it started, if I heard it correctly, what month did you join the Republika Srpska army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-48
utterances.text: It was in April. That was the beginning of the organisation of the army. At first as civilian protection and then some units were formed of men of military age. I already told you how many people lived there. At the beginning there were maybe about 900 people, but because of the terrible positions and large casualties, this number went down, and at the end of the war there were less than 100 soldiers there of those who were there at the beginning of the war as the local residents.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What happened to the rest?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-48
utterances.text: Well, many were killed. I can now --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, it is not so important. It doesn't matter. Could you tell me, what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-48
utterances.text: The attacks on the neighbourhood were frequent. Many people were killed or wounded. I can tell you for myself my -- my family, we had four members in our house. My mother was killed in a shell explosion in 1993 and my father was killed in 1995. My sister left for security reasons, and I was the only one that was left in the house, and that's happened in other families too. Civilians left because of their safety especially on the front line, because most of the buildings there were torn down or burnt down. It was so unsafe to move about. It was impossible to move about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But could you please tell me there and then at the beginning in April and May, what was there in terms of weapons? What did you -- when you took up a rifle, what did you -- what kind of weapons did you have?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-48
utterances.text: Well, we had some infantry weapons and some mortars. We had two armoured personnel carriers. Because we were encircled, they were not really able to function. They were used to neutralise sniper nests in the buildings around us. Often they targeted the 18th floor of the blue building at Alipasino Polje. They would often put a machine-gun there and then they would fire on the entire neighbourhood. We asked for help then to neutralise this firing position, at the beginning, until all the weapons were taken away, and then we found ourselves in a very unenviable situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And when were the weapons pulled out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-48
utterances.text: Well, I can't tell you with any certainty. There were some agreements. That's what I do remember. That was in late 1993. I can't really remember with any certainty. Maybe early 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And if you can recall perhaps what did the year 1994 look like?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-48
utterances.text: Well, 1994 was much calmer in this area, unlike on other front lines which were very, very active. Even though we had so few people, we gave our support at Trnovo and Ilijas, because military offensives at that time took place outside of Sarajevo, the Sarajevo theatre was relatively calm.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me, when you talk about Nedzarici, you showed us where Nedzarici is. Could you please tell us what is Nedzarici, what part of this area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-48
utterances.text: Well, it is it part of the Novi Grad municipality in the city of Sarajevo which is located between Alipasino Polje and the Sarajevo airport. It's just a neighbourhood in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And in the time of war, could you get out --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic and the witness, please pause between question and answer. You're overlapping.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You said that there were 900 soldiers there and then what you said, lest we should repeat it, and there were 4.000 people, 700 families. So from that area, was it possible at all to go anywhere in any direction and if yes, how?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-48
utterances.text: At the beginning, we used the route that led across the airport in Sarajevo. After the agreement and the handing over of the airport to the international forces, we had very -- it was very difficult for us to communicate with the rest of our territory. We had just one very narrow passage leading through Kasindolska street, and then through Ilidza, Vogosca, Poljine, and then a path that led through the woods, which was really not very adequate. So to go a distance that is maybe four to five kilometres, that used to be four to five kilometres, we had to travel about 100 kilometres. This was particularly a problem when somebody would get seriously injured. But people would mostly not survive this trip to -- to the hospital because -- at the Zica hospital, it was not possible to carry out major surgeries.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-48
utterances.text: If I may --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. Please just follow what I ask you. When was it possible to pass through Kasindolska street, at what time of day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-48
utterances.text: During day-time it was very difficult. One did it at one's own risk. Any travel took place mostly at night, although you had to drive with your headlights out with maximum precautions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please, you spoke about 1994 and those events that -- the fighting that happened in other areas. What part of those conflicts, what part of the areas did you go in relation to those conflicts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-48
utterances.text: You mean in 1994?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-48
utterances.text: In late 1994, I went to the Trnovo theatre where there was major offensive --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-48
utterances.text: -- of our forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have hesitated up until now, but this evidence, in my submission, is irrelevant to the charges against the accused and the Prosecution has on umpteen occasions conceded that there was a conflict ongoing, and so the evidence that a soldier went to Trnovo to participate in combat operations, I submit, is irrelevant to the matters at hand and especially because Trnovo is beyond the geographical scope of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How do you respond, Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I will put things very simply today, because you know that -- and I have to say that now, the indictment has been amended one month before the beginning of the trial, and it would be the simplest thing for the Defence to call the witnesses of the type that we -- that our previous witness was. I could have called any number of them. I had to take into account the amended indictment where it -- which is based on the allegation that General Dragomir Milosevic inherited all those things that had been done in the previous period and continued with all that in one sense. I started paying a lot of attention to that, so I no longer dealt with that time-period, and I still don't know what the Defence is to deal with it, what the scope of it is. So I have been following and complying with the suggestions that I received, and I tried to get-- I'm trying to get from the witness how he started being involved in war, and what happened until that period when General Milosevic took on his duty. Now he started talking about a lull, where there were no major military activities or casualties in the area where he lived, but then he moved to another theatre, and I'm trying to prove, the Defence is trying to prove that at the time while Dragomir Milosevic was in command, there was no strategy of campaign for the eight months of that period until May and there was no campaign there, either, but then there was this major offensive launched by the BH army and now the Defence is trying to strictly comply with this framework and to indicate just to certain elements that preceded that, and I don't know whether, until the end, it will turn out that the time that preceded the times relevant for the indictment is also important because if the indictment continues to allege that Dragomir Milosevic inherited everything that happened in the previous period, in the terms of the campaign and the events, then I simply cannot see why I'm not allowed to mention 1992, 1993, and even 1994 until sometime, I don't know what time, August 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva, the point Mr. Tapuskovic is making or one of the points is that there's an allegation in the indictment that General Milosevic inherited the campaign of General Galic and therefore he should be entitled to deal with the pre-indictment period, starting from 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, that's correct and, for the record and although I submit the indictment is clear, that our case is that the accused inherited a campaign of sniping and shelling that was perpetrated by General Galic and not only did he inherit it, but he continued to order for it -- he ordered for it to continue during his time as a Sarajevo-Romanija Corps commander. And so, of course, the time-period before the actual indictment period where General Milosevic was the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps commander is relevant in that respect. And we also submit that the -- that pre-indictment period is relative to the notice of General Milosevic. But I didn't object on that ground. I objected on the grounds of a witness coming here who actually is from Nedzarici, which is an area that is critical to the Prosecution or to the case at hand, talking about Trnovo, which is actually beyond the geographic scope of the indictment and beyond the geographical scope of the indictment against General Galic. And from what I can gather, the witness was about to speak to combat activity in Trnovo, which the Prosecution has never -- never, you know, objected against that. There was a war going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How far is Trnovo from the confrontation lines? Can the witness assist us? Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Line of confrontation or from this part, this area where I was?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, tell us from both.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Trnovo is about 15 kilometres from Sarajevo. It's a Sarajevo municipality, as far as I know. I mean, I lived there, I mean in Sarajevo, so I don't know what the problem is. The line -- so Trnovo is some 15 kilometres from where we were. The line changed in relation to the Trnovo front. At the beginning, Trnovo -- of the war, Trnovo was first under the -- under the control of the B and H forces when awful massacres were committed against the Serb population. Then after the liberation, proof was found, bodies and so on and so forth. So Trnovo itself was the site of fighting and then the line kept getting closer and closer to Trnovo as the war went on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, how is Trnovo relevant to the indictment? Just explain quickly. Don't have a long introduction. Just tell us summarily how it is relative, considering the distance that we have just heard that it is from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will answer very briefly, Your Honours. Sarajevo is not the only town in the world that is spread over an area of 15 to 20 square kilometres. There a many towns that spread to a length of 15 to 20 kilometres. Sarajevo has a tram that went to Ilidza or Vogosca, so all of that is the town of Sarajevo, and unless we understand that, and until we understand that, I will really have to explain that every day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I said I'm going allow to you deal with it, but deal with it briefly and move on. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is the essence, Your Honours. The area of responsibility of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and the area of responsibility of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the sectors that constitute the territory of Sarajevo and where the Sarajevo citizens live. This is all mixed together and you couldn't separate anything to -- in terms of saying this is Sarajevo and this is not. Nedzarici is the heart of Sarajevo. Grbavica is the heart of Sarajevo. It was all mixed together and it is our thesis, well, of course, Your Honour, Judge Harhoff you don't like to hear this, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation ...] That you are going to lead to adduce is simply evidence of Serb suffering. You know that that is not enough. It has to have some additional element that links to the charges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And, Mr. Tapuskovic, please excuse me. There is no question of me not wanting to hear evidence in this case, provided it is relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So, as I said, deal with it, but deal with it briefly and move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we submitted a motion about this and if I have to provide explanations like this every day in relation to positions that we have already stated, I'm going to strictly stick to things that are directly linked to all of the events, primarily the events that have to do with the incidents, but the incidents and I repeat that again, are something that the Defence will -- in relation to these incidents, the Defence would prefer best if we could only stick to the incidents and nothing more because in that case it would be the easiest thing for the Defence. The questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Didn't you understand? I said you -- I allowed you to question the witness about this matter but briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I understood that I needed to provide another brief explanation, but I'm actually not able to provide any explanations about anything anymore, anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, when did these offensives end in 1994?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-48
utterances.text: The offensives around Sarajevo in 1994 were constant and then they moved in mid-1995 to the Sarajevo --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please, please. I asked you a simple question, when all of this finished in 1994.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-48
utterances.text: In 1994 specifically, about the situation that I talked about, they finished, we actually stopped their forces at the Trnovo front.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what does the time now look like in 1995? Can you establish a time-period until when things were quieter.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-48
utterances.text: In the beginning of 1995 things were more quiet but we did have some indications of an offensive towards our sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what did you in Nedzarici -- and what did you do in Nedzarici in the situation when you were finding out that an offensive was being prepared?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-48
utterances.text: Due to the lack of heavy weaponry, we were forced --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva. Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I rose because I wasn't sure whether the witness in his previous answer was speaking to Trnovo or Nedzarici, but I understand that he was speaking with respect to Nedzarici. No objection.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And can you please go on and tell us what did you do in Nedzarici in that quiet period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-48
utterances.text: We were trying to fortify as best we could. We were carrying out engineering work like any regular army. We were fortifying, making screens for visual protection. On one occasion my father --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Just one moment. And what happened in the month of May?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-48
utterances.text: In May, during this engineering work, my father was killed by a sniper shot near the faculty of theology because that road was directly endangered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, as -- again, and this is meant in no way disrespect to the witness, but the evidence regarding the suffering of Bosnian Serbs in Nedzarici, in my submission, is not relative to the charges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I imagine that is it just an incidental matter, and you're going to move on to the area of his evidence that is very relevant to the charges, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I said "incidental" --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Sorry. Just a minute. When I say "incidental," I don't mean to say that it was not an important event for the witness whose father who was killed and he has my full sympathy. But let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What I wanted to hear from you, you were talking about engineering works in order to protect yourself from the attack.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-48
utterances.text: For purposes of defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, for purposes of defence, but what was happening? I don't want to ask anything about the suffering of your father. What happened in the month of May? Were there any events that had something to do with combat?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-48
utterances.text: Combat actions started in late May against our positions and then they escalated in June and early July. There was a lot of strong artillery fire, sniper fire continuously.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to speed things up so we can finish early today. I would like to show you a document since what you already said that. It's a Defence exhibit, D159. Witness, sir, can you please read loudly the heading of this document, what this document is, first of all, and who signed this document, but read it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-48
utterances.text: Command of the 12th division, strictly confidential, number 02/2-2-182. Sarajevo the 4th of July, 1995. I think that's the year. You cannot really see it clearly. I don't see the signature here. The commander of the 1st Corps is what it says at the top. I cannot see the entire page, so I cannot see the bottom -- oh, all right. Commander Brigadier Fikret Prevljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can you please read now --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-48
utterances.text: Just one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. Just a moment. Can you please now read item 1, paragraph 1?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-48
utterances.text: During the period from the 15th of June to the 3rd of July, 1995, we fired from all types of weapons we had at our disposal over 300 VT of the enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And the last paragraph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-48
utterances.text: We believe that the number of destroyed and damaged VT combat and non-combat materiel is larger because we acted during conditions of limited visibility at night, so we did not have the opportunity to observe everything entirely.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Before you read this, can you please tell us what you started to say earlier and that is to tell us about what you experienced throughout these 15 days?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-48
utterances.text: First of all, it wasn't just 15 days. In early June, I happened to just stay alive. Fortunately, there is a kind of hole there --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right, all right, very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to show you another document. It's Defence exhibit 160.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is no English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I recall that the English version is the next page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see. So may we have the English version which you say is on the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I understand it to be, yes, Mr. President. And-- I'm sorry, I'm sorry to my learned friend. But for the benefit of the Court, you will see that the point 1, there is no translation, and I have a translation of that portion, which in my submission, is important for understanding this document. So I have copies for -- for Your Honours and for Defence counsel, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. Did you hear that, Mr. Tapuskovic? Point 1 is blank, but Mr. Sachdeva has a translation of it, English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I am very glad, because given the circumstances that I was in when I got the document, I had to translate only the parts that were relevant for me, but of course we need a complete translation, so this is great.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Let's have the English translation of paragraph 1 and then we can proceed to paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, could you please do the same thing that you did just a little while ago. Read the heading and what it says underneath it and the first paragraph in item 2, that's where it says "our forces."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-48
utterances.text: Second -- 12th division command, strictly confidential, number 02/2-2/166, Sarajevo, the 1st of July, 1995, operational time, 1600 hours. Now, who signed the document, I can't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could we perhaps scroll down a little bit.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-48
utterances.text: Commander Brigadier Fikret Prevljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-48
utterances.text: Our forces --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Our forces and the first and the second passage in this paragraph. Out loud.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-48
utterances.text: The unit is in full combat readiness. The most salient artillery fire was opened on the sector of Nedzarici barracks with 80-millimetre mortars and 100-millimetre mortars where we structured a fire to disrupt the enemy engineering works, and with the same target we opened fire from 105-millimetre Howitzers and the T55 tank twice on Gucica hill. All the fire was carried out with great accuracy.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This is it precisely what you have just told us that you were at Gucica Hala. You said that you were next to it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-48
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me what you've just read here. Is this what happened that day and how -- what did it look like?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-48
utterances.text: It more or less correspond to what happened. In the actual fact one of our soldiers was killed and two were very seriously wounded. They had to have their limbs amputated. And this was an everyday occurrence in that period of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-48
utterances.text: That preceded the offensive that was attempted against us, against our positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And could you tell me something about those demarcation lines, something about blind people's home, did a blind people's home exist, and what kind of a building it was in the moment that we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-48
utterances.text: The blind people's home was a building, a two-storey building at the top of Nedzarici, it was in our territory on the ground floor -- well, it is a building that is very close to those apartment buildings that I mentioned at the beginning, Vojnicko Polje, Alipasino Polje, and then also Oslobodjenja, and the nursing home to the right. That's a new building that had never -- nobody had lived there at all. It was in -- under their control and this building was -- was constantly under fire, under terrible fire throughout the war and people mostly stayed in the basements.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: At the very start you said that Nedzarici was a settlement with low buildings. You've already explained that. What did the other buildings nearby look like?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-48
utterances.text: Well, these were high-rise apartment buildings up to 18 storeys high and then in relation to those family homes, that would have the ground floor and the first floor or even just a ground floor. There were just a couple of buildings that had three storeys. So the sites held by the army facing us were much higher so they were in an extremely better position than we were. They had more places from which they could observe, target us. They had a line of sight from those high-rise buildings over the whole area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have just two more questions. The first is: What do you know by the faculty of theology? What kind of a building is that and is there anything that is important from the beginning and at the end of the war that you took part in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-48
utterances.text: That building was closer to the lower-lying end of Nedzarici, close to the airport, in relation to Vojnicko Polje, it was about a kilometre and a half away.
